newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma rice exports limited by slew of obstacles.
newsitem.headline: Burma rice exports limited by slew of obstacles.

text.p: Despite having a great deal of potential, Burma has a long way to go before it can emerge as a major rice exporter, analysts said on Thursday.
Ineffective government policy, a lack of adequate infrastructure and poor milling techniques remained major obstacles, they said.

"Burma certainly has natural resources, the land and the water to be able to produce a lot of rice. They have a good potential in increasing their productivity and probably their exports," said a senior U.S. Embassy agriculture official based in Bangkok.
"But their agricultural policies are limiting their ability to increase their productivity," said the official, who asked not to be named.
The military government's price control scheme, a policy requiring farmers to sell part of their output to the government well below the market price, has exacerbated the problems.
"These problems are compounded by poor infrastructure, inefficient milling capabilities, which effect the quality of rice, and insufficient fertilizer," he said.
"All these problems will make it difficult to achieve their potential," he added.
Trade sources said the fact that the government controls the rice exports could make Burma's rice prices unattractive, not reflecting the market trend.
"The government sometimes prices the rice too high to move the market," said one trader with a U.S. trading house.
Burma currently exports mostly 15-20 percent grade and broken rice. Its buyers include Indonesia and African countries.
Its rice exports this year are expected to plunge to 300,000 tonnes or less from an estimated 645,000 tonnes in 1995, the U.S. Embassy agricultural attache said on Thursday.
"Concerns over depleting stock levels forced the Burmese government to slow down exports this year after selling aggressively in 1995," he said.
But the trend is likely to improve in 1997 when the exports are expected to rise to around 500,000 tonnes, he said.
However, the production forecast is expected to be revised as pessimism about wet season crop, to be harvested chiefly in November and December, appears to be growing.
This is due in part to unseasonably late rains into the first week in November, which once again threatened to reduce yields and milling outturn, he said.

The country's rice exports during the first 10 months of 1996 amounted to 261,692 tonnes, a 59 percent drop from the same period last year, according to a report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
